record.title: Dynamo paper reports GPU-resident state reuse cuts LLM-serving recovery to seconds
record.summary: A Sept. 21 preprint from NVIDIA authors presents GPU Memory Service (GMS), initialized-runtime snapshots and Shadow Engines for recovering LLM inference replicas without reloading model weights when a worker process fails but its GPU remains intact. Across four eight-GPU model configurations on vLLM and SGLang, the paper reports Shadow Engine recovery in 4.6–6.2 seconds, 12.8–29.0× faster than a warm restart. A separate replay of the authors’ production failure trace estimates 79% of recovery-related GPU-hours could be reclaimed. These are author-reported results for device-preserving process failures; device loss and broader deployment behavior remain open.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The preprint presents a recovery design combining initialized-engine snapshots, GPU Memory Service (GMS) for persistent read-only model allocations, and a preinitialized Shadow Engine.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across four eight-GPU model configurations on vLLM and SGLang, the authors report Shadow Engine recovery in 4.6–6.2 seconds, or 12.8–29.0× faster than their warm-restart baselines.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Replaying an 18-week production failure trace, the authors estimate the design could reclaim 79% of GPU-hours lost to recovery.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_LIMITATION
claims.text: The reported fast path covers device-preserving engine-process failures; device-invalidating failures require rebuilding model state, and the production savings result is a replay estimate rather than prospective live deployment measurement.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of latency, memory overhead or production-trace savings was established in this activation.

brief.importance_rationale: If fast recovery works across production workloads, it could materially improve inference availability and reduce capacity held to mask warm-restart windows. Score 6 reflects this systems-level consequence under device-preserving failures, not independent confirmation or universal transfer.
limitations: Results are author-reported and have not been independently reproduced in this activation.
The 12.8–29× figures are for eight-GPU replicas and injected engine-process failures where GPUs and model allocations survive; a device failure follows a slower rebuild path.
The comparison uses cached weights/compilation for warm restart; the paper says this is optimistic relative to most trace recoveries, but benchmarks remain specific to the tested systems.
The 79% GPU-hour benefit is estimated by replaying one production trace, not by a prospective deployment experiment.
Shadow engines consume 4.3–8.1 GiB per GPU in tested configurations; this is not literally zero-cost standby capacity.
brief.summary: A Sept. 21 preprint from NVIDIA authors presents GPU Memory Service (GMS), initialized-runtime snapshots and Shadow Engines for recovering LLM inference replicas without reloading model weights when a worker process fails but its GPU remains intact. Across four eight-GPU model configurations on vLLM and SGLang, the paper reports Shadow Engine recovery in 4.6–6.2 seconds, 12.8–29.0× faster than a warm restart. A separate replay of the authors’ production failure trace estimates 79% of recovery-related GPU-hours could be reclaimed. These are author-reported results for device-preserving process failures; device loss and broader deployment behavior remain open.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report 12.8–29.0× lower recovery latency than warm restart across four eight-GPU model configurations and estimate 79% of recovery-related GPU-hours could be recovered on an 18-week production trace.
technical.compute_or_cost: Shadow Engine standby adds 4.3 GiB/GPU for Qwen3.8-27B and 7.4–8.1 GiB/GPU for larger tested models, trading KV-cache headroom for recovery speed.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper specifies and implements the above components. In the reported test setup, GMS + Shadow Engine recovery measured 4.6–6.2 seconds across four vLLM and four SGLang model/configuration rows; independent execution was not performed here.
technical.implementation_status: Paper reports implementations in Dynamo, vLLM and SGLang; code links are linked from the paper, but no build or independent reproduction was run in this activation.
technical.mechanism: Snapshots capture initialized engine runtime state while excluding request KV pages; GMS owns physical model-weight allocations outside engine processes so they survive device-preserving process failure and can be reattached read-only; a Shadow Engine shares model state and is promoted after failure, leaving recovery mainly to allocate fresh KV backing and register with the serving plane.
technical.regime: Eight GPUs per replica; Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro across vLLM 0.27.1 and SGLang 0.5.18. Evaluated failure injection kills engine process trees while devices and resident allocations remain; separate device-invalidating recovery is slower.
technical.reproducibility: Paper contains configuration and workload details; code availability is indicated by authors. Independent reproduction and assessment of deployment prerequisites remain open.
technical.strongest_baseline: Warm restart with model weights already in host page cache and compilation artifacts cached; authors describe this as optimistic relative to most recoveries in their production trace.

brief.title: Dynamo paper reports GPU-resident state reuse cuts LLM-serving recovery to seconds
brief.why_it_matters: If the reported results transfer to live serving, preserving resident model allocations while rebuilding runtime state could reduce capacity loss and spare-GPU overprovisioning for fault-tolerant inference. The immediate consequence is strongest for clusters where process failures leave devices and allocations healthy; this does not establish recovery from GPU/device failure.
